summary: Interview with Adv. Ilit Ostrovitch-Levi, director general of Israel's Money Laundering and Terror Financing Prohibition Authority (IMPA), on the financial fight against Hamas since October 7, 2023. She describes real-time international blocking of fundraising, a 900% rise in terror-financing reports, and Hamas funding methods such as hawala, trade and online crowdfunding. She argues Iran is the core funder and that only global sanctions can end terror financing.
one_line: IMPA chief Ilit Ostrovitch-Levi explains how Israel and international partners block Hamas funding pipelines, and why Iranian financing needs global sanctions.
key_facts: IMPA received secret intelligence from two European countries two weeks into the war that a large organization was raising funds for Hamas via social networks and fintech platforms under the guise of Gaza donations; one country froze its financial activities immediately, without court orders.
Ilit Ostrovitch-Levi has headed IMPA since May 2022.
Before October 7 IMPA received about 100 terror-financing reports a day; the number jumped to about 1,000, a 900% increase.
Three days after the war began, IMPA called on all global regulated entities to increase vigilance toward terror financing and report suspicious activity.
According to IMPA, the Iranian budget to Gaza is in the order of $100 million a year, most of it going to Hamas's military wing.
The main method of transferring money to Gaza is hawala, in which money changers settle accounts internally without cash physically crossing borders.
In August 2021 the NBCTF, AMAN and the Tax Authority seized 23 tons of chocolate bars at the Nitzana Border Crossing, suspected of being bought with terror financing funds for Hamas.
Hamed al-Khachari, a Gazan money changer who worked for Hamas, combined trade and hawala in a scheme involving Turkey; Israel assassinated him in 2019.
On October 18 OFAC sanctioned 10 key Hamas operatives and financial facilitators; on October 27 it imposed a second round of sanctions including a Hamas official in Iran and IRGC members.
Andrea Gacki, director of FinCEN, contacted Ostrovitch-Levi three days after the war began and offered full support, leading to an unprecedented flow of US financial intelligence.
Heads of the Netherlands' and Germany's anti-money-laundering authorities proposed an international task force with Israel and the US that meets every few days to exchange intelligence.
Intelligence reports from parallel foreign authorities rose from about 24 a month before the war to about 50.
Ostrovitch-Levi says Hamas continues fundraising in Judea and Samaria and online, including fictitious projects like throw-pillows and jewelry, to fill reserves for 'the day after'.
She argues the lasting solution is global sanctions through FATF and OFAC, since 'without money there is no terrorism'.
